awd_titl_txt: Conference Support for the Haleakala Neutron Monitor Workshop; Honolulu, Hawaii; January 2025
awd_abstract_narration:
The Haleakala Neutron Monitor Workshop will be held in Honolulu, Hawaii, in January 2025. The workshop will bring together approximately 50 participants from Hawaii, mainland USA, Thailand, Mexico, and other countries to celebrate the installation of two neutron monitors at the Haleakala summit. These monitors provide unique capabilities for observing galactic cosmic rays and solar neutron particles, contributing valuable data for studying cosmic ray physics, atmospheric interactions, and radiation hazards. This workshop will bring together experts, early-career scientists, and engineers to foster collaboration, exchange knowledge, and address key scientific questions about particle propagation, solar events, and nuclear interactions in Earth’s atmosphere.

The five-day workshop, to be held at the University of Hawaii at Manoa and Haleakala, will feature plenary talks, technical sessions, and a site visit to the Haleakala summit for a ribbon-cutting ceremony and tour of the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST). The final day will focus on exploring synergies between neutron monitor data and DKIST’s solar science objectives. Early-career participants will have the opportunity to present research in plenary sessions and engage with senior scientists, building connections across neutron monitoring, space weather, and atmospheric science.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
In January 2025, with support from the National Science Foundation, the University of Hawai‘i at Mānoa hosted the Haleakalā Neutron Monitor Workshop and Ribbon Cutting Ceremony. This event marked the scientific inauguration and operational integration of two newly deployed neutron monitor stations—HLEA and THIMON—at the summit of Haleakalā on Maui.

Neutron monitors are ground-based instruments that measure secondary particles produced when high-energy cosmic rays from space interact with Earth’s atmosphere. These measurements are essential for understanding space weather—conditions driven by the Sun that can affect satellites, aviation, navigation systems, communications infrastructure, and power grids. The Haleakalā stations are located at high altitude and at a favorable geomagnetic position, making them especially sensitive to changes in Galactic Cosmic Rays and solar particle events.

A major outcome of this award was the successful integration of HLEA and THIMON into the Simpson Neutron Monitor System, the U.S.-operated network of neutron monitor stations managed by U.S. institutions. During the workshop, scientists coordinated calibration procedures, detector response modeling, and real-time data contribution pathways to ensure that the Hawai‘i stations meet operational standards within this system.

In parallel, data from the Haleakalā stations are being shared with the Neutron Monitor Database (NMDB) and the broader global neutron monitor network, which aggregates measurements from stations worldwide. This integration ensures that radiation measurements from Hawai‘i contribute both to U.S.-based monitoring efforts and to international space weather research.

Importantly, the workshop reinforced the role of the Space Weather and Mission Control Center (SWMCC) at the University of Hawai‘i at Mānoa as one of two primary hubs for collecting, validating, and distributing data from the Simpson Neutron Monitor System. The SWMCC in Hawai‘i now serves as a central node for data ingestion, quality control, and dissemination, strengthening U.S. leadership in coordinated space weather monitoring and ensuring reliable data flow during periods of heightened solar activity.

From an intellectual merit perspective, the workshop strengthened scientific coordination during the current solar maximum—a period of increased solar activity when radiation events are more frequent and intense. Technical discussions improved alignment on detector response functions, atmospheric corrections, normalization procedures, and cross-calibration requirements. These efforts enhance the scientific reliability of neutron monitor data used to study cosmic ray modulation, solar energetic particle events, and solar-terrestrial interactions.

The broader impacts of this award are significant. First, it strengthened U.S. ground-based space weather infrastructure by expanding the Simpson System with high-altitude coverage in Hawai‘i and by reinforcing SWMCC as a national data coordination hub. Improved geographic coverage and centralized data management enhance the ability to detect and characterize radiation events that may affect aviation routes, satellites, and technological systems.

Second, the workshop supported workforce development. Undergraduate and graduate students participated in scientific sessions, presented research contributions, and interacted with senior scientists from universities and national laboratories. Early-career researchers gained exposure to practical challenges in detector operations, calibration methodology, and real-time data integration. These experiences contribute directly to training the next generation of scientists in experimental astrophysics and space weather research.

Third, the event increased public awareness of space weather science. The ribbon-cutting ceremony at Haleakalā and related outreach activities highlighted the societal importance of radiation monitoring and infrastructure resilience. Publicly accessible videos and online workshop materials extended the reach of the event beyond the scientific community.

Although this award supported a conference rather than new construction or laboratory experimentation, its impact lies in coordination, collaboration, and infrastructure integration. By convening experts from universities, national laboratories, and international institutions, the workshop accelerated the full operational integration of Hawai‘i’s neutron monitors into the Simpson System and strengthened connections to NMDB and the global network.

Overall, this NSF-supported workshop advanced scientific collaboration, enhanced U.S. space weather monitoring infrastructure, supported student development, and reinforced Hawai‘i’s role as a strategic center for radiation monitoring and data coordination.
